title: Containers and the Reproducible Deployment
html:
Containers and the Reproducible Deployment

A service can pass every test and still fail after deployment when the test environment differs from the production host. The code revision may be identical while the runtime libraries, configuration, filesystem permissions, or available CPU and memory differ. A Git revision alone does not tell us what was actually running.

This distinction became difficult to ignore during a Catalog Service deployment at Baodium. The deployment record showed one Git revision across the fleet, yet some instances served requests successfully while others failed during startup. The engineers compared the failing hosts with the serving hosts. One had an older system library, another used an older language runtime, and a third lacked a required environment variable. The same application revision was being started under several combinations of runtime inputs.

Containers address part of this problem by packaging application files and runtime dependencies. A Linux container runs processes on the host’s kernel, with filesystem, process, and network isolation provided through namespaces. Processor time and memory are constrained separately, through cgroup limits that the deployment has to set: a container without them competes for the host’s resources like any other process, so the limits in Section \(\ref{sec:ch06-limits-config}\) have to be chosen and configured explicitly. Because the kernel is shared rather than emulated, starting a container is closer to starting a process than to booting a machine, and a kernel-level difference between hosts still reaches inside one.

Repairing the affected hosts would restore the immediate deployment, but another release could encounter the same differences. Baodium moved toward immutable image promotion, separate environment configuration, and readiness checks that reflected whether an instance could actually serve requests. The distinction between the image and its deployment environment remained essential because the kernel and resource limits still came from the host.

Application Source and Runtime Inputs

A Git revision identifies a source tree. It does not identify the Python interpreter installed on a host, the native library loaded by a package, or the configuration injected when the process starts. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch06-layers}\) separates the three.

For instance, a Python dependency may call a compiled library. The application can import successfully on one host and fail on another because the required library version is absent. A successful start on the first host does not establish that the second host has the required library version.

This gap is where “it works on my machine” lives. The revision is identical on both machines, and everything that differs sits in the layers underneath it. These differences are often described as environment drift. The failure may be entirely repeatable on each affected host, even though it appears inconsistent when engineers compare only application revisions.

Baodium divided the runtime inputs into those that should travel with the application and those supplied by the deployment.

The image packages one portion of the runtime contract.
Packaged with the application Supplied at deployment or runtime
Application files and dependencies Configuration and secret references
Language runtime and user-space libraries Host kernel and CPU architecture
Default filesystem layout and permissions Mounted files and writable storage
Default process identity and startup command Resource limits, networking, and platform policy

A container image contains the packaged files and default execution settings. A running container is a process, or group of processes, started from that image with additional runtime configuration. For ordinary Linux containers, the processes use the host kernel. The image supplies the user-space environment, including libraries and utilities, rather than a separate running operating-system kernel. This division gives us a more precise investigation. If two instances use the same platform-specific image, we can compare their configuration, mounts, limits, and host conditions without first reconstructing every application dependency.

Building the Deployable Artifact

The Catalog team changed its release process so continuous integration (CI) built the application and its user-space dependencies into an image. Hosts no longer installed those dependencies independently during deployment.

A simplified Dockerfile follows:

[
  language=bash,
  caption={Packaging Catalog Service with declared build inputs.}]
# CI supplies an approved base reference pinned by digest.
ARG PYTHON_BASE_IMAGE
FROM ${PYTHON_BASE_IMAGE}

WORKDIR /app

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

COPY requirements.lock .
RUN python -m pip install \
    --no-cache-dir \
    --require-hashes \
    -r requirements.lock

COPY catalog_service ./catalog_service

USER 65532:65532

CMD ["python", "-m", "catalog_service"]

The base image supplies the Python runtime and its user-space dependencies, and pinning its digest fixes the selected base content. The lock file pins the application dependencies, including transitive dependencies, and provides hashes for the permitted package artifacts.

The service files are copied explicitly rather than taking every file from the working directory. This reduces the chance of including local credentials, test output, or unrelated files. The build context also excludes those files through its ignore configuration.

The numeric user runs the service without root privileges. Files needed at runtime must therefore be readable by that identity, and any required writable directories must have suitable ownership. The final command uses the executable form so the runtime starts Python directly. Shell wrappers require care because they can interfere with signal delivery unless they replace themselves with the application process.

Test the built image’s permissions, startup command, native libraries, and packaged files. Unit tests run directly on the CI host do not exercise those parts of the image.

Build Inputs and Updates

Pinning dependencies makes a build easier to explain, but it also means updates need an explicit process.

Pinning has a cost. A pinned dependency changes only when someone rebuilds the image, so a security patch published today reaches production only after that rebuild. Teams that pin without scheduling rebuilds trade an unpredictable failure for a predictable one, which is an improvement only if the rebuild actually happens. The usual remedy is a recurring job that bumps the pinned references, runs the tests, and opens a change for review, so that dependency updates are reviewed regularly rather than a decision anyone has to make.

A base-image patch does not appear in an existing image. The team updates the approved base reference, rebuilds, tests, and publishes a new artifact. The same applies to application dependency fixes.

Build tools can introduce additional inputs. If installing a package compiles native code, compiler versions and build dependencies matter too. Projects that require such tooling can use a separate build stage and copy only the runtime artifacts into the final image.

The release record includes the source revision, base-image reference, dependency inventory, and build provenance. An image digest identifies content, but does not by itself establish who built it or whether it passed the required checks.

Artifact Promotion

Once CI has built and tested an image, the release pipeline needs to identify that exact artifact. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch06-promotion}\) contrasts building a separate image for each environment with building once and promoting that image.

A tag such as catalog-service:release-42 is a useful name, but registry policy may permit someone to assign it to another image. A digest identifies the referenced content. If you keep one habit from this section, make it this: deploy by digest, and treat tags as labels for people. A tag is a name that someone can move; a digest is a fingerprint, and a fingerprint cannot be reassigned.

Baodium recorded the published digest in the release manifest and promoted that reference through test, staging, and production. Production did not rebuild from the source revision. Why does this matter if the source is unchanged? A second build can select a changed base image, resolve another package version, use another compiler, or include generated metadata. Testing one build does not validate all later builds from that source.

Promoting the recorded artifact removes that uncertainty from the release path. Producing identical output from a repeated build is a separate reproducible-build goal that requires control over all relevant build inputs.

Multi-platform images add another detail; a single image index can reference distinct images for different CPU architectures. Deployments using both architectures need to validate those platform-specific images and record which one each instance actually runs.

The release pipeline also checks the deployed digest to confirm which image the requested tag resolved to. Registry retention preserves previously approved artifacts for rollback.

Configuration Outside the Image

Database endpoints, feature settings, credentials, and resource allocations differ between environments. Packaging production values into the image would prevent the same artifact from being promoted unchanged. Baodium therefore versioned deployment configuration separately; a release identified the image digest and the configuration revision used with it. This separation would have exposed the missing environment variable in the original incident. The application also needed to reject invalid configuration before accepting customer work.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Validating configuration before the service becomes ready.}]
def load_config(env):
    required = ("DATABASE_URL", "REDIS_URL")
    missing = [name for name in required if not env.get(name)]

    if missing:
        raise ConfigError(
            "Missing required configuration: "
            + ", ".join(missing)
        )

    try:
        pool_size = int(env.get("DB_POOL_SIZE", "40"))
    except ValueError:
        raise ConfigError("DB_POOL_SIZE must be an integer")

    if not 1 <= pool_size <= 40:
        raise ConfigError(
            "DB_POOL_SIZE is outside the approved range"
        )

    return Config(
        database_url=env["DATABASE_URL"],
        redis_url=env["REDIS_URL"],
        pool_size=pool_size,
    )

The pool range is an application-specific constraint; validation should also cover formats, incompatible options, and required files. A value being present says nothing about whether the endpoint is reachable or the credentials work, so those checks belong to initialization or dependency handling.

A startup failure identifies the invalid field without printing its value, which is especially important for connection strings that contain credentials. The team also distinguished malformed configuration from temporary dependency unavailability, because a missing required value cannot be repaired by retrying a network call. A temporarily unreachable database may justify bounded initialization retries or a non-ready instance, depending on the deployment policy.

Secrets and Configuration Changes

Secrets are supplied through the deployment’s approved secret mechanism. They are excluded from image layers, build arguments, diagnostic dumps, and command-line arguments that may be recorded. If a credential enters an image layer, deleting it in a subsequent layer does not remove the earlier content. Copies may exist in registries, build caches, and nodes; the response includes credential rotation and an investigation of those copies.

Secret rotation also needs an application rule. Updating a mounted file does not establish that the process has reloaded it, and an environment variable does not change inside an existing process merely because the deployment definition changed. For each configuration class, the team specifies whether changes require a restart or support validated reload. The process reports the configuration revision actually in use, without exposing secret contents.

Isolation and Writable State

Container isolation limits which host resources a process can see and how it can use them. Linux namespaces provide separate views of resources such as processes, mounts, and networking. Cgroups account for and constrain resource consumption.

The exact isolation depends on runtime configuration. Containers sharing a network namespace, such as containers in the same Kubernetes Pod, also share its port space. Host mounts or elevated privileges can grant access beyond what the image alone suggests.

For Catalog Service, the runtime used a non-root identity, restricted capabilities, and explicit writable locations. A read-only root filesystem helped expose accidental writes to application directories during testing.

The writable layer of a container is not a durable application store. Replacing the container can discard those changes. Catalog Service therefore stored business records externally and treated local files as temporary or reconstructable.

This affects application design in ordinary ways. A generated report needed durable object storage if customers were expected to retrieve it later. A local cache could be discarded, but its refill work needed the admission controls from Chapter 5.

Temporary storage also needs a limit and monitoring. A service can fail because logs, downloads, or temporary files exhaust available space even when its CPU and memory measurements appear acceptable.

CPU and Memory Configuration

Containers make resource settings explicit, which means those settings become part of the conditions tested before release. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch06-limits}\) lays out what each kind of exhaustion looks like.

In Kubernetes, a resource request informs scheduling and resource allocation; a limit constrains consumption. A CPU limit can cause throttling, while memory exhaustion can lead to process termination.

These settings should come from measurements of the service under representative work. Copying values from another application can create failures that look like code regressions.

CPU Throttling

Suppose Catalog Service passes a load test without a CPU limit, then runs in production with a restrictive quota. The process may need more CPU time than that quota permits during parts of the scheduling interval. The kernel delays further execution when the quota is consumed. Requests can take additional time without an application exception, even when the node has unused CPU capacity. What makes throttling confusing is that, from outside, nothing crashes and no error appears. Requests take longer, and a dashboard that shows CPU against the whole node can look unremarkable.

The investigation compares throttling measurements, the configured quota, request volume, and CPU time per request. A quota change is appropriate when the service needs that CPU and the placement can support it. An unexpected increase in CPU per request also requires examining the application change.

Throttling alone is not a complete diagnosis. The team treats throttling as an incident only when it coincides with degraded request completion.

Memory Exhaustion

Memory includes more than the application’s managed heap. Native allocations, thread stacks, buffers, runtime overhead, and memory-backed temporary storage can contribute to the container’s usage. If a language runtime is allowed to use the entire container limit for its heap, these other allocations may cause termination before the application considers its own heap exhausted.

The mismatch is easy to create and hard to see in testing, because a test machine rarely enforces the same limit that production does. The engineers therefore measured memory under realistic concurrency, large responses, and sustained operation. They left space for non-heap use and checked whether memory returned after work completed.

An out-of-memory termination needs evidence from the platform and node. Exit status 137 alone only indicates a process killed by SIGKILL in common reporting conventions; it says nothing about why the signal was sent.

Termination reason, memory usage, configured limits, node events, and restart timing help distinguish container-limit exhaustion from node-wide problems or an external kill.

Raising the limit may accommodate legitimate demand. It will only postpone failure if the application continues retaining memory without a bound.

::: decision

**Should readiness check the database?**

Catalog Service cannot serve most of its endpoints without PostgreSQL. A reviewer proposes that the readiness probe run SELECT 1 against the database, so an instance that has lost its connection stops receiving traffic. The service runs twelve replicas behind one load balancer.

**Yes. An instance that cannot reach the database should not be sent requests.**

**No. Keep readiness local and let requests fail with a clear error when the database is unavailable.**

**Yes for a new instance during startup, no afterwards.**

—

A can help when one instance has lost database access and other instances can still serve the request. During a shared database outage, however, all twelve probes could fail and remove every endpoint, including those that could serve reduced responses or database-independent requests. Repeated probe queries also add work to the dependency.

B preserves those response paths during a shared outage. It still needs a way to detect an instance-specific fault, such as a damaged client pool, and to decide whether removing that instance would improve service. An alert reports the fault. The serving layer removes an instance only when its routing policy instructs it to do so.

C checks initial connectivity but cannot detect a later instance-specific failure; the startup probe in this chapter checks local initialization. Adding a database check would be a separate policy choice and would need bounds on query frequency and startup waiting.

Choose readiness behavior by testing both failures: one isolated instance and the shared database. Route requests to instances that can serve the required response, including an approved fallback. No single dependency probe establishes that for every endpoint.

:::

Startup, Readiness, and Liveness

A process can be running without being prepared to accept the traffic assigned to it. Catalog Service needed configuration validation, local initialization, and usable database access before serving its initial requests; it did not need every optional cache entry to be populated.

Use a separate check for each decision. Startup gives initialization time to finish, readiness decides whether this instance should receive new traffic, and liveness tests a condition for which restarting this container is an appropriate recovery action. An unavailable database usually belongs in dependency handling, because restarting every client will not repair it.

Probe results have different operational consequences.
Check Question Consequence of failure
Startup Has initialization completed under its allowed startup period? Continued failure can trigger restart.
Readiness Should this instance receive service traffic? The serving layer withdraws it from eligible endpoints.
Liveness Is the process in a condition that warrants restart? Continued failure can trigger restart.

A startup probe allows initialization to finish before normal liveness and readiness probing begins, and its allowance should cover measured startup variation.

Readiness describes whether the instance can serve its assigned role; a process that has not loaded required configuration should not become ready. A populated optional cache may be unnecessary if bounded source reads can support the initial load.

Liveness should avoid treating a shared dependency outage as a reason to restart every instance. Restarting Catalog Service does not repair PostgreSQL, and simultaneous restarts can add connection creation and cache loading to the outage.

Readiness dependencies require judgment too; if one instance has broken local connectivity, removing it from service may help. If every instance loses the same dependency, removing every endpoint may prevent the application from returning useful degraded responses.

Probe design follows the service’s permitted outcomes. The endpoint should report the state relevant to that decision, using inexpensive checks that do not themselves generate substantial dependency work.

Warm-Up and Initial Traffic

Readiness and full operating capacity are not necessarily reached at the same instant. A new process may have few established database connections, an empty local cache, or a runtime that has not completed frequently used compilation paths. Its first requests can therefore consume more work than requests to an established instance. Once readiness succeeds, the serving layer may send the instance its full traffic share. A full share requires the instance to support that load immediately; a controlled introduction permits some initialization to continue while traffic increases.

An arbitrary count of open database connections is a weak readiness rule. Connections need to be usable, and the count should be justified by initial demand and connection-establishment cost. Opening the entire pool before serving may waste sessions and create a startup burst.

Warm-up work is bounded alongside live work. New instances, existing instances, and terminating instances can all use the same database during a deployment.

A shared Redis cache does not empty when one application process restarts. Local caches do, so any warming plan must identify which cache actually needs population.

For a Kubernetes rollout, a configuration such as the following controls planned replacement:

[
  language=YAML,
  caption={A rolling-update policy with limited surge.}]
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0

This requests no planned reduction in available replicas and allows a limited surge during replacement. It does not guarantee that only one extra process is using resources at every instant. Terminating Pods may still consume resources, and autoscaling, node replacement, or another deployment can introduce additional work. The database allocation must account for those overlaps.

If no node has space for the surge Pod, the rollout may stall. That is preferable to assuming that a desired replica count proves replacement capacity exists. Deployment strategy is examined further in Chapter 10.

Shutdown and In-Flight Requests

A shutdown signal can arrive while requests are executing. The instance needs to stop accepting work and give admitted requests a bounded interval to finish.

Starting the right artifact is only half of replacement; the old process also needs to stop without abandoning work unnecessarily. Catalog Service handles termination by marking itself unavailable for new traffic, draining accepted requests, closing clients, and exiting under a bounded shutdown deadline.

Endpoint withdrawal is not instantaneous across every proxy or client, and existing connections may also continue delivering requests. The application and serving layer need compatible draining behavior in addition to the readiness change.

The process must receive and handle the termination signal. This is another reason to test the actual entrypoint and any wrapper scripts in the image.

If a request cannot finish before forced termination, the outcome depends on the operation. A read can fail and be retried under its caller policy; a payment write may require the durable reconciliation procedure from Chapter 3.

Increasing the termination grace period can allow more draining, but also extends the interval during which old and new instances consume resources together. Shutdown duration belongs in the deployment capacity calculation.

A replacement test therefore sends representative requests while terminating an instance. It checks errors, unfinished operations, resource release, and the time until the process exits.

Rollback and External State

An image digest makes the earlier application artifact retrievable without rebuilding it. That is useful only if the artifact can still operate against the current environment. Suppose a release renames a database column and removes the old name. Restoring the earlier image can start the old process successfully, yet its first query may fail because the expected column no longer exists. Before any release that touches stored data, ask what the previous version would do with the data the new version has written. If the team cannot explain how the previous version will read that data, rollback has not been validated.

Compatibility must cover the period when old and new code can both execute. An expand-then-contract migration introduces a compatible schema, deploys code that uses it, migrates data, and removes the earlier form only after the approved rollback period ends. Messages and cache formats require the same attention. An old consumer may encounter events published by the new release, and an old reader may encounter cached values written by it. Rollback therefore records more than the previous digest; it identifies compatible configuration, available secret references, schema assumptions, and external interfaces. Restoring old secret references must not undo a required credential revocation.

The rollback test runs representative requests through the previous artifact against the state expected after the new release has executed. A clean startup is no promise that rollback will restore service.

The image change also does not reverse business effects already completed by the newer code; those effects require their own migration, reconciliation, or compensation procedure.

Deployment Evidence and Failure Investigation

The value of a deployment record is decided months later, by whoever is trying to work out what changed.

The original incident required engineers to inspect hosts because the release record identified only the application revision. The revised record included the image digest, source revision, configuration revision, resource settings, and platform-specific artifact. Startup events recorded the runtime placement and initialization result.

This information supports a focused comparison, and the comparison is quick enough to make during an incident. The commands below are all read-only, which matters when the instinct under pressure is to restart something before anyone understands what differs.

[
  language=bash,
  label={lst:ch06-verify},
  caption={Read-only checks that separate an artifact difference from a
           configuration difference from a host difference.}]
# 1. Is every running pod on the same image digest?
#    imageID carries the digest; image may show a mutable tag.
kubectl get pods -l app=catalog \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{..imageID}{"\n"}{end}' \
  | sort | uniq -c

# 2. Did the rollout finish? How many replicas are new?
kubectl rollout status deploy/catalog --timeout=0s
kubectl get rs -l app=catalog -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,WANT:.spec.replicas,\
READY:.status.readyReplicas

# 3. Same config? Compare mounted resource versions.
kubectl get cm catalog-config \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion}{"\n"}'

# 4. Are failing pods clustered on one node?
kubectl get pods -l app=catalog -o custom-columns=\
POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,\
READY:.status.phase | sort -k2

# 5. Why did a container stop? Exit 137 with OOMKilled
#    is a memory limit, not an app exception.
kubectl get pod "$POD" -o jsonpath='{range\
 .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.lastState.terminated.reason}\
 {.lastState.terminated.exitCode}{"\n"}{end}'

# 6. What did the platform observe, not the app?
kubectl get events \
  --field-selector involvedObject.name="$POD" \
  --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

The order is deliberate. Each step removes one explanation, which narrows the set of causes the next step examines. If step 1 shows two digests, the question is about rollout state and the remaining steps are premature. If the image digests and configuration revisions match, the engineers investigate differences in host configuration and runtime conditions. Step 4 checks whether the failure occurs on one host or several.

If failures cluster on one node despite matching artifact and configuration identities, they investigate node resources, kernel and runtime conditions, mounts, and networking. A common image can still interact badly with one host condition; matching digests narrow the investigation without proving the application is uninvolved.

Diagnostic output excludes secret values; configuration comparisons use names, presence, approved nonsecret fields, and versioned references. Dumping the entire environment into logs can turn a deployment investigation into a credential exposure.

Release verification uses the built image under the intended user identity, filesystem permissions, and resource limits, and it also exercises startup, readiness, termination, and rollback.

The rollout controller or release automation needs an explicit action when those checks fail. A reported progress failure does not necessarily initiate rollback by itself. The release procedure defines when to stop further replacement and how to preserve the evidence needed for investigation.

Summary

Catalog Service ran from the same source revision on every host, yet some instances failed during startup because their libraries, language runtimes, and configuration differed. Rebuilding the code from the same commit could not establish that the tested application was the application running in production. Packaging the runtime dependencies into a versioned image made artifact identity verifiable across environments.

The image is one part of the deployed service. The host kernel, resource limits, secrets, network configuration, persistent state, and workload traffic still come from the environment in which the container runs. Readiness must indicate whether an instance can serve real requests, and termination must give it enough time to stop accepting new work and complete or recover operations already accepted. Rollback also requires compatibility with external records created by the version being replaced.

A useful deployment test follows one instance from build to startup, warm-up, sustained traffic, and termination, then tries the previous image against the new version’s external state. Chapter 7 examines another deployment assumption that an image cannot settle: whether a read from a replicated database reflects the write the customer has just completed.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & The tested image, combined with validated configuration and declared runtime conditions, can support the traffic assigned to each instance.
Condition that tests it & A deployment changes configuration, resource limits, or probe outcomes.
Constraint or invariant & The image contains application user space. The deployment and host supply configuration, mounts, kernel behavior, resource enforcement, networking, and external services.
Evidence and uncertainty & The original failures were confined to hosts with different system libraries, language runtimes, or required configuration, despite a shared application revision.

Whether initialization, resource limits, host differences, and current external state permit the approved artifact and its rollback version to serve representative requests.
Signal and evaluation window & Compare image digests and configuration at release. Measure throttling, OOM events, and readiness through rollout.
Control and decision & Promote the tested artifact by digest with versioned configuration. Admit traffic only after the required initialization checks, and verify replacement and rollback against current external state.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner defines initialization, readiness, shutdown, and compatibility requirements. The platform owner manages artifact delivery, runtime policy, placement, and resource enforcement. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
:::
